what_it_did.what_the_split_means: A mechanical commit republishes an unchanged net -- the report, the dashboard, the state files. Counting those as work would make a quiet day look busy, so they are separated rather than filtered: they happened, they are just not progress.

what_it_decided.thesis_read: The thesis has a reading again and it is a loss, and this time the loss is real rather than plumbing. The A/B was re-run on the repaired chain: the control arm reproduces bit-identically (net GBP 1,145,681.029513 in both runs), so the arm is the only thing that changed. Every mechanism fix worked exactly as designed -- `clamped_by_the_price_cap` falls 27 to 0, so the cap now binds inside the search instead of landing afterwards; `ceiling_bound` fires 20 times where it was structurally unable to fire at all; declines rise 3 to 10 as the arm refuses renewals it cannot lawfully price; and the median chosen margin more than halves, GBP 100.50 to GBP 39.75/MWh. And the loss barely moved: net -GBP 91,742 and enterprise value -GBP 110,731 over ten years, against -GBP 118,252 before, a 6.4% improvement. The arm halved its price and lost the same money, which retires over-pricing as the mechanism and means the honest sentence today is that the company's per-customer arm loses to its own flat rule on realised P&L. Two things qualify that and both are work rather than caveats. First, of 69 renewals seen the arm chooses freely on 21: 36 land on a bound, 20 at the ceiling and 16 at the floor, plus 2 extrapolation- bound. On a capped domestic book the regulator and the floor make most of the decisions, and that is a finding about what a per-customer arm can even do here. Second -- and this is the centre -- the belief it maximises against carries no per-account lifetime information at all. Recovering the hazard from EP1's own published output, all 33 graded accounts return the identical 0.05 and a flat 20-year tenure: one distinct value across the whole graded population. So whatever ranking that CLV produced came entirely from the margin term, and the lifetime half of "lifetime value" is a constant. The hazard is `0.05 + 0.03 x bill_shock_count`, a step function of one integer that is zero for 42% of all renewal decisions in the run. The thesis says the advantage must come from INFERENCE; on the dimension the whole thesis is named after, there is currently no inference to have an advantage from. That also corrects me: I sent the last stretch at a five-fold inflation in the lifetime term, and the term is not inflated -- believed hazard 0.05 against a realised 0.053 in the bucket every graded account sits in, and portfolio believed tenure 11.74 years against a realised implied 13.82. It runs SHORT, and the defect is absent dispersion, not wrong level. The 2.529 gap is also partly the yardstick: the graded population is selected on the outcome, like-for-like resi excluded-over-graded is 2.96x, and a point-in-time-fair divisor gives 2.193 rather than 2.529. Finally, the headline loss cannot yet be attributed to anything: the arm gives up GBP 123,006 of gross margin on 3 extra churns, which is GBP 41,000 a churn against domestic accounts averaging ~GBP 420 of whole-life margin, so it cannot be three domestic customers -- and the instrument built to say which accounts it was reports `largest_single_difference_gbp: 0.0` because every per-account figure in it is null and the aggregation sums nulls to zero. Nothing went backwards. The project is materially more honest than it was three hours ago and commercially exactly where it was. On the previous direction the record is good: all four items were worked, the Lane 0 progress signal and the A/B re-run both landed, EP1 was advanced by a worker that overturned my diagnosis rather than executing it, and EP13 moved twice without reaching the rung I named. This is the first orientation where the delivery lane's own progress signal can be trusted, because `record_landing` now binds real paths to each claim.

focus.what: Land the churn-roster-diff instrument and make it capable of reporting a number. Three things are uncommitted in the working tree right now and they are the whole instrument: `tools/run_value_cycle_ab.py` (modified -- `git show HEAD:tools/run_value_cycle_ab.py | grep -c churn_roster_diff` returns 0), `tests/tools/test_run_value_cycle_ab.py` (untracked), and `docs/observability/value_cycle_ab.json` (modified -- the 13:58:01Z run, identical in every realised figure to the committed 12:35:29Z one, differing only by carrying the new block). Commit them by pathspec. Then fix the defect the output shows: `churn_roster_diff` names five accounts -- C1_2, C3, C6, C7 lost under the value arm and PROS-2019-0003 under the control -- and every one has `segment: null` and `realised_lifetime_margin_gbp: null`, while `only_in_value_arm_realised_gbp`, `only_in_control_arm_realised_gbp` and `largest_single_difference_gbp` all read 0.0. The per-account entries correctly declare a blank; the aggregation collapses those blanks to zero, so the verdict is a constant no run can move, and it is published beside a `reading` that instructs the reader to divide it into `realised_delta.gross_margin_gbp`. Two halves, both needed: make the arms publish `per_customer_lifetime` so the figures exist at all (`tools/run_value_cycle_ab.py:163` reads `result["per_customer_lifetime"]` and falls back to `phase2b`; `margin_movers` is unavailable for the same reason), and make the aggregates unavailable rather than 0.0 when they are summing blanks. R15 both ways: a mutation proving a genuine single-account concentration is reported, and a null control proving an all-blank input reports unavailable instead of zero. Then re-run and say which accounts moved the GBP 123,006.
focus.why: The only measurement this project has of its own thesis is -GBP 110,731 of enterprise value, and nobody can currently say whether that is a portfolio property or one decision. The arm loses GBP 123,006 of gross margin on 3 extra churns -- GBP 41,000 each, against domestic accounts whose whole-life margin averages about GBP 420. This book carries five I&C accounts averaging GBP 221,491 of lifetime margin and the four accounts the value arm lost differently are all C-prefixed. If the delta is one large account then "the value arm loses" is a case study and n=1 is not a thesis; if it is spread, the loss is a portfolio result and everything downstream reads differently. This is first because it is the cheapest item here and it decides how to read every other item, and because the instrument that would answer it is a control whose verdict cannot vary -- the fourth R15 shape, on the measurement that matters most. It is also the same lesson this stretch already learned twice: `6089f90a9` and `5a2caf338` landed because a paired reading was only as committed as its weaker half, and two commits later the entire instrument is sitting in one worktree again. Finished when the tool, its test and its output are in origin, an all-blank input reports unavailable rather than 0.0, both directions are proven by tests, and the record names the accounts behind the GBP 123,006 or states with figures that no single account dominates it.

focus.what: Give the tenure horizon per-account dispersion it does not have, from observables the company can actually know. The measured fact to work from, not to re-derive: `docs/observability/coupled_gap_ledger.json` `components.lifetime_level` reports `distinct_hazards: 1`, `hazard_histogram {"0.05": 33}`, `hazard_is_constant_across_graded_population: true`, median believed tenure 20.0 years for every graded account. The cause is `saas/churn_model.py::churn_probability` -- `min(0.05 + 0.03 * bill_shock_count, cap)`, a step function of one integer that is zero for 42% of the run's 622 renewal decisions -- consumed by `company/analytics/clv_three_horizon.py` at H2 as `hazard = latest.churn_probability`, with the term `1.0 / hazard`. Do NOT re-diagnose the level: `hazard_calibration` grades belief against a tally of `event_type` and the 0.05 bucket reads 0.05 believed against 0.053 realised over 263 decisions, so the level is right and the dispersion is what is missing. Widen the propensity to use more of what a supplier observes about an account -- payment method and payment behaviour, tenure to date, the account's own tariff against the market it could switch to, consumption volatility, contact and complaint history -- and check every input against the wall before using it: if it needs a simulation internal it is a violation, and `company/interfaces/sim_interface.py` is the only door. Then re-measure with `python3 -m tools.couple_clv` and report the ledger's next reading whichever way it moves. Nothing may be tuned toward a smaller gap (R12), and the 0.204 scalar is not to be applied. If the gap worsens, that is the result and saying so is the deliverable. A level move to 3 is available on this evidence if the coupled rung is genuinely met -- self-certify with `record_level_up_self_certified`, and never `--no-verify` a `level_current` change.
focus.why: This is the thesis, stated as a defect. The director's thesis is a supplier deciding customer-by-customer on lifetime value, beating a flat baseline through better prediction and nothing else -- and on the lifetime half of that sentence the company currently predicts the same 20-year life for every customer it grades. A constant cannot rank anything, so whatever per-customer view the value arm has today comes entirely from the margin term, and the arm that loses GBP 110,731 is maximising against a belief that is flat on the axis the thesis names. It is second only because item one decides whether that loss is a portfolio property, and it is not fourth because every other measurement in this project ultimately grades this estimator. It is also the first lead here that is a real inference problem rather than an instrument repair: the hazard is not wrong, it is uninformative, and making it informative from observables alone is exactly the work the thesis says the advantage has to come from. Finished when the graded population shows more than one distinct hazard, the ledger's next entry comes from a changed estimator rather than a changed sample, every new input is named with the observable it comes from and cleared against the wall, and the new gap is recorded whichever direction it went.

focus.what: Decide the divisor and then ratchet the class. I decide the first half here so nobody has to ask: the published no-skill baseline moves to the point-in-time-fair one -- the mean realised value of accounts that had ALREADY ceased when each belief was formed -- and the in-sample figure is published beside it, not deleted, so the two readings stay comparable and the change is legible in the record. Both numbers already exist for EP1: 2.529 in-sample against 2.193 point-in-time-fair, so about 13% of the headline is the yardstick and the belief is still worse than no-skill either way; this is not an acquittal and must not be presented as one. The reason it is a decision rather than a diagnosis is that it moves a published figure, which is mine to take and is taken. Then do the class work `WORKER_FINDING_THE_CLV_GAP_IS_GRADED_ONLY_ON_THE_CUSTOMERS_WHO_LEFT_2026-08-26.md` leaves open under R10: `tools/couple_supply_start.py` normalises against "predict the mean tenure", and `couple_pb3_book_growth.py` and `couple_value_based_pricing.py` also publish an in-sample `g0` -- none has been checked for whether its graded population is selected on the outcome it predicts. Walk all fifteen `tools/couple_*.py`, and make the general rule enforceable rather than remembered: a no-skill baseline computed on the graded population is not no-skill, so any coupler publishing a `g0` must publish the selection profile beside it or fail. Reuse `tools/clv_gap_selection.py`, which already does this for EP1 and already has its six proven mutations.
focus.why: The coupled-triad doctrine says the gap IS how this project judges itself, and sixteen atoms are graded by that ledger. EP1 has just shown what a contaminated one looks like: a perfectly calibrated hazard scored as a five-fold over-estimate because the harness graded the model on precisely the 5% who left, and that single artefact aimed a whole stretch of thesis-critical work at the wrong term -- mine, and the closing report to the director. If any other coupler grades an outcome-conditioned population, the number the director reads as "the company's belief against the world" is partly the yardstick, and we would not know which. This is third rather than first because EP1's contamination is now measured and declared, so nothing is currently being misread; but it is on the list rather than in the tail because it is the instrument every other item is measured with. Finished when the published EP1 divisor is the point-in-time-fair one with the in-sample figure beside it, every `couple_*.py` has been walked and its answer recorded, and a control fails a coupler that publishes a `g0` without the selection profile that lets a reader judge it.

focus.what: Build the coupler. There are fifteen `tools/couple_*.py` and none is carbon; `docs/observability/coupled_gap_ledger.json` has sixteen keys and none is EP13; the atom is still `level_current: 2`. The independent truth series exists -- `sim/neso_carbon_intensity.py`, NESO's published half-hourly number, deliberately a separate module from `sim/grid_carbon_intensity.py` so the two routes stay independent -- and it has never been used to grade anything. Write `tools/couple_carbon_intensity.py` in the shape of its siblings, measure the gap between the company's reconstructed intensity shape and NESO's published series, and write the row into the ledger. Read focus item three before choosing the divisor: do not publish a `g0` fitted on a population selected by the thing it predicts. The specific claim to confirm or correct in figures is the one `sim/grid_carbon_intensity.py` makes about itself in its own L2 ledger entry -- that its quietest half hours sit near 0.05 of average against NESO bottoming out nearer 0.16, because no coal and no interconnector imports are dispatched, so any time-shifting benefit computed from it is an upper bound. That sentence is a recollection written in the grammar of a measurement. Move `level_current` to 3 and self-certify with `record_level_up_self_certified` only if the gap is measured and the atom's three named L2 reservations are answered; if the gap is large the level stays at 2 and saying so with the figures is the deliverable. Never `--no-verify` a `level_current` change.
focus.why: This atom was named last orientation, drawn, and two substantive commits landed against it -- the biomass envelope measured and deliberately not dispatched, the actionable forecast graded as a ceiling -- and the rung that actually gates the level was not the one built. Under the coupled-triad rule no world atom reaches 3 until the company has been tested against it and the gap measured, so this is the one atom on the board whose level can move on real evidence rather than on a landed file. It is fourth because it is world fidelity rather than the supplier's per-customer inference, and the three items above are all on the thesis itself. It is on the list at all because it is the same discipline in a cleaner instance: a number published without the independent comparison that could refute it, with the refuting series already built and sitting unused. Finished when the ledger carries a carbon row produced by a coupler that reads both series, the 0.05-against-0.16 claim is confirmed or corrected in figures, and the level either moves with that evidence cited or is explicitly held with the reason written down.

what_next.why_this_is_here: Direction multiplies the draw's existing weights and can never zero one, so it can only ever be ignored -- never obeyed by force. Whether it was actually followed is therefore a measurement, not an assumption.
